title: Wood provision
text: This page describes the method of the wood provision accounts as the tool implements it. Each step points to the stage of the tool that carries it out, and the code annex at the end describes each stage with links to its code. The numbers and tables that a run produces are in the report of that run, in outputs/wood/report/, which carries the same method text together with them.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.1 Overview
The accounts deliver four groups of quantities for every reporting year. The actual flow is the net annual increment (NAI) of the forest available for wood supply. The sustainable flow is the part of the wood removed from that forest that stays within the increment, and overuse is the part that exceeds it. Each of these is reported in cubic metres and in euro, in current prices and in constant prices of 2010. The quantities come in two forms, as tables by country (NUTS0) and by NUTS2 and NUTS3 region in an Excel workbook, and as maps on a grid of 100 m cells. The section on products at the end describes both.
Forest statistics report these quantities by country, and they do not say where in the country the wood grows. The work therefore runs in four steps, which the sections below follow in order.

Eurostat statistics give the NAI and the removals of each country and year, and the gaps in them are filled by rules that the section on the actual flow explains.
Comparing removals with the NAI gives the sustainable flow and the overuse of each country.
A unit value in euro per cubic metre, built from timber and export prices, turns the physical quantities into values.
A spatial key, which combines where forest grows with how productive the vegetation is, shares each national value among the regions and the 100 m cells of the country. Regions and cells therefore add up to the national values.

The accounts cover the EU27 with the NUTS 2024 boundaries, at the country level, NUTS2 and NUTS3 (Eurostat GISCO, 2024). See the stage prepare in the code annex. The boundaries carry the notice © EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries. All grids use the projection EPSG:3035, in which every cell covers the same area on the ground. Malta has no forest available for wood supply and no forestry activity (Vallecillo et al., 2019), so its values are zero throughout.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.2 Actual flow
The source of the actual flow is the table for_vol_efa of Eurostat, which collects the European Forest Accounts in thousand cubic metres over bark (Eurostat, 2026e). It holds the NAI and the removals of each country, both for the forest available for wood supply (FAWS) and for total forest (FOR) (see the stage accounts in the code annex). It needs completing, since few Member States report the NAI of forest available for wood supply in the early years.

1.2.1 Filling the gaps
INCA Part III fills the gaps with the estimates of the carbon budget model of the JRC, which simulates the growth of the forests of each country from their inventories (La Notte et al., 2021; Pilli & Grassi, 2021). These estimates are published in a workbook that combines the model with the forest accounts and gives the total NAI of each country from 2000 to 2019, with the values after 2016 held at their level of 2015 (see the stage prepare in the code annex). The series refers to total forest, and the workbook also gives the share of available forest in the growing stock, so two versions of the fill are possible. The INCA tool uses a third, the NAI of total forest reported to Eurostat. Each run compares all three with the values by Member State printed in the annexes of Part III, which are the published reference for the method (see the stage accounts in the code annex).
 The total forest estimate of the carbon budget model follows the method that Part III states and reproduces its Member State values best, so a decision was made to use it. The NAI is therefore taken in this order. A value reported for available forest comes first. The carbon budget estimate comes next. Any remaining gap takes the mean of the nearest earlier and later values of the same country, and gaps at the end of the series repeat the last value.
The carbon budget estimate covers total forest and fills a statistic of available forest, so it probably overstates the flow in the countries that take it. Each run measures this effect against the EU27 aggregates that Eurostat publishes, which it estimates itself.
Eurostat holds few values for the last reporting year, and the method says nothing about how far a value may be carried. A decision was made to carry the last value, since the increment changes slowly and any trend applied to it would add an assumption that the data cannot support.


1.2.2 Changes of source within the series
A Member State that starts reporting available forest moves from the estimate of the model to its own figure, and the two can differ widely. We kept the series as the method builds it and did not adjust the model estimates to the reported levels, so changes over time within these countries should be read together with the list of these changes in the report of each run.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.3 Sustainable flow and overuse
The accounting reports class wood among the services with a regeneration rate that use can exceed (La Notte et al., 2021), and the handbook of ecosystem accounts describes overharvesting as removals above the NAI (Eurostat, 2026a). Neither gives a formula for wood, so we adapted the one of Part III for water purification, in which overuse is the difference between the actual and the sustainable flow and the threshold defines the sustainable flow. Regeneration is the threshold for wood, which gives these two equations for each country and year.
\[
\text{Overuse} = \max(\text{Removals} - \text{NAI},\ 0)
\tag{1}\]
\[
\text{Sustainable flow} = \min(\text{Removals},\ \text{NAI})
\tag{2}\]
Removals are the removals of available forest in for_vol_efa, which Member States report more widely than the NAI. They take the same rule for gaps, with reported removals of total forest in place of the model estimate. The two quantities add up to the removals in every country and year (see the stage accounts in the code annex). A single year above the threshold can be a temporary peak, for example after a storm, and the handbook treats overharvesting as a matter of an extended period, so the results also show the ratio of removals to NAI of every country and year.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.4 Monetary valuation
The value is the physical quantity times a unit value in euro per cubic metre. INCA Part III derives the unit value in three steps (La Notte et al., 2021). The output of forest trees in for_sup_cp (Eurostat, 2026d) divided by the NAI gives the unit value of the NAI, which few Member States report in the early years. The roundwood exports of for_basic (Eurostat, 2026c), in value and in volume, give a unit value for most countries and years, but this price includes the harvesting and transport added on the way to the market. The ratio between the two then carries the export price back to the standing tree.
\[
\text{Ratio}_{c,t} = \frac{\text{Unit value of exports}_{c,t}}{\text{Unit value of NAI}_{c,t}}
\tag{3}\]
\[
\text{Completed unit value}_{c,t} = \frac{\text{Unit value of exports}_{c,t}}{\widehat{\text{Ratio}}_{c,t}}
\tag{4}\]
Where the ratio is missing, \(\widehat{\text{Ratio}}\) takes the mean ratio of the country, or the EU mean if the country has no ratio at all (see the stage accounts in the code annex). Gaps in the export price take the same means. Means run over 2000 to 2023 for a country. The EU mean takes the mean of the countries in each year and then the mean of those years from 2012 to 2023, where coverage is better, as in the INCA tool.

1.4.1 Screening the ratio
The ratio is very sensitive to small denominators. An output of forest trees recorded close to zero yields a very large ratio, which drives up the EU mean, so every Member State that takes the EU mean would end up with a unit value close to zero.
The INCA tool removes all the timber values of Croatia, Finland, Greece, Portugal and Sweden and the export points of Denmark in 2014 and Greece in 2006 (European Union, 2026), and we did the same. The data used here are more recent than that list, so it does not catch everything. A decision was made to extend the rule in a way that the data support. A Member State whose median ratio falls below 1 or above 100 loses all its timber values, and any single observation outside that range is dropped. The lower bound follows from the meaning of the ratio, since a standing tree cannot be worth more than the harvested roundwood.
Export prices have their own errors. A decision was made to drop a point that lies more than three times above or below the median of its country, a rule that also catches the Greek point of the INCA tool.


1.4.2 Constant prices
Part III moves its other accounts to constant prices, so that the accounts follow changes in the service and leave aside changes in the market (La Notte et al., 2021). It does not state a deflator or a price basis for wood. The accounts therefore report both current and constant prices. Constant prices multiply the value of each year by a deflator, which is the HICP of the EU27 (Eurostat, 2026b) rebased to 2010. A single EU27 index and the base year 2010 are a method choice that keeps all the accounts of this series on one price basis, and the INCA tool uses national indices with base year 2000 instead.
Overuse and the sustainable flow take the same unit value as the NAI of their country and year, since the method has no separate price for them.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.5 The spatial key
Part II spreads national flows over the forest of Corine Land Cover in proportion to Dry Matter Productivity (Vallecillo et al., 2019), and the Earth observation roadmap of the INCA project keeps a forest mask and that proxy (Zurbarán Nucci et al., 2025). The weight of a 100 m cell in year \(t\) is therefore
\[
w_{i,t} = F_{i,t} \cdot P_{i,t}
\tag{5}\]
where \(F_{i,t}\) is 1 for forest in the Corine accounting layer of the year (European Environment Agency, 2026) and 0 elsewhere, and \(P_{i,t}\) is the annual productivity resampled to 100 m with bilinear interpolation (see the stage prepare in the code annex). A cell then receives
\[
\text{Value}_{i,t} = \text{Value}_{c,t} \cdot \frac{w_{i,t}}{\sum_{j \in c} w_{j,t}}
\tag{6}\]
so the cells of a country add up to its national value. The maps use these 100 m weights directly. The regional tables use the same weights added up to 1 km, as the section on regional tables explains (see the stage maps_100m in the code annex).
Forest mask. Part II limits the mask to the broad-leaved, coniferous and mixed forest classes (311, 312 and 313) and leaves out transitional woodland and shrub (324) (Vallecillo et al., 2019). The INCA tool includes that class, so the two differ, and a decision was made to follow the report.
Availability. The mask holds all forest, available or not. Part II tried to delineate available forest through slope and protected areas and rejected this, because thresholds differ across countries and the result can mislead (Vallecillo et al., 2019). A map of available forest now exists for 2020 (European Commission, Joint Research Centre, 2026), and a decision was made to leave it out. It covers one year in a series of five, the reports do not call for it, and the statistic that is spread already refers to available forest.
Productivity. Part II and the roadmap name Dry Matter Productivity. This work uses Gross Dry Matter Productivity, a separate Copernicus product that also counts the autotrophic respiration of the plants, because it was the product at hand and the other needs a further bulk download.1 The proxy only shares a national value among the cells of a country, so what matters is the relative pattern within a country and national totals do not depend on it. The 1 km product, version 2, serves 2000, 2006 and 2012 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-c), and the 300 m product, version 2, serves 2018 and 2024 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-d).
A test then measured what this choice costs (see the stage prepare in the code annex). It compared the Dry Matter Productivity products (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-a, n.d.-b) with half of the gross products, since the quality page of the 1 km product describes a constant fraction of 0.5. It covers 10 of the 180 pairs of files behind the key, namely the files ending on 10 January and 10 July of each reporting year, over the whole of Europe. The tolerance was set before the comparison. In every pair, the absolute difference could reach 1.0 percent of the productivity total, and the cells with data in only one product could reach 0.1 percent of the cells. Dry Matter Productivity equals exactly half of the gross value in every cell, with data in the same cells. A constant ratio leaves the share of every cell unchanged, so on this evidence the two products give the same key, and the key stays on Gross Dry Matter Productivity. The other 170 pairs were not compared, so the finding rests on this sample.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.6 Regional tables
The value of a region is the national value times the share of the region in the weight of its country in that year, so the regions add up to the country and follow the same key as the maps (see the stages prepare and accounts in the code annex). Shares are computed on the 1 km weights, the sum of the 100 m weights in each 1 km cell. All regions of a country therefore share one unit value, and the overuse of a country reaches all its regions in proportion to their weight, since the data do not show where removals take place inside a country.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.7 Products
Workbook. The workbook holds one sheet for each group of quantities and NUTS level. The sheets of the actual flow give the NAI in thousand cubic metres, and those of overuse give the sustainable flow and the overuse side by side. The monetary sheets give million euro in current prices and in constant prices of 2010. The reporting years are the columns, and a first sheet explains the contents.
Maps. There are six maps for each reporting year on the 100 m grid, built with the 100 m weights of Equation 5. See the stage maps_100m in the code annex. They hold the actual flow, the sustainable flow and the overuse, each in physical terms and in constant prices of 2010, which gives 30 maps. Each cell holds a whole number in small units, cubic decimetres of wood or euro cents. Whole numbers make the files several times smaller than decimals, and every country keeps its total to within one part in a thousand. The files are Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF without overviews, which keeps them small, and a GIS such as QGIS draws them quickly as they are.
Working layers. The run also spreads the actual flow and its value over the 1 km weights. These 1 km layers are not a product of the accounts. They give the map figures of the report, drawn at 10 km, and a check of the 1 km weights against the national values. See the stage maps_1km in the code annex.

title: Wood provision
text:
1.8 Checks
The run stops when a check fails and records the result. The 100 m maps are added up by country from the whole numbers as they are written, and compared with the national values country by country. See the stage maps_100m in the code annex. The 1 km layers are read back from disk and compared in the same way. The run also stops if the NUTS2 and NUTS3 totals differ from the NUTS0 totals in any table, metric or year.

title: Carbon sequestration
text: This page describes the method of the carbon sequestration accounts as the tool implements it. Each step points to the stage of the tool that carries it out, and the code annex at the end describes each stage with links to its code. The numbers and tables that a run produces are in the report of that run, in outputs/carbon/report/, which carries the same method text together with them.

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.1 Overview
The accounts deliver five quantities for every reporting year. The flow without offset is the CO2 that land removes from the atmosphere. The actual flow is what remains of those removals once the emissions of land are compensated, and it is the service that reaches society. The missed flow is the difference between the two, which is the part of the removals used up by emissions. The actual flow and the missed flow are also valued in euro. Each quantity is reported in two forms, as tables by country (NUTS0) and by NUTS2 and NUTS3 region in an Excel workbook, and as maps on a grid of 100 m cells. The section on products at the end describes both.
National greenhouse gas inventories report CO2 by country and land category, and they do not say where on the land it is taken up. The work therefore runs in four steps, which the sections below follow in order.

The inventory gives the removals and the emissions of each land category in each country and year.
The offset nets all emissions against all removals across the European Union, and the result is shared among countries. This gives the actual flow, the flow without offset and the missed flow by country.
A price per tonne of CO2 turns the flows into values, in current prices and in constant prices of 2010.
A spatial key, which combines where forest grows with how productive the vegetation is, shares each national value among the regions and the 100 m cells of the country. Regions and cells therefore add up to the national values, and they show where within a country the service is most likely to occur.

The analysis covers the EU27, by country, NUTS2 region and NUTS3 region under the NUTS 2024 boundaries (Eurostat GISCO, 2024). The boundaries carry the notice © EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries. All grids use the projection EPSG:3035, in which every cell covers the same area on the ground (see the stage prepare in the code annex).

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.2 Removals and emissions
We took CO2 by source sector from the Eurostat dataset env_air_gge (Eurostat, 2026b) for the 27 Member States and the EU27 aggregate (see the stage accounts in the code annex). This dataset carries the national inventories that countries report under the climate conventions, and its part on land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF) gives the CO2 that each land category exchanges with the atmosphere. Following Vallecillo et al. (2019), the land categories are forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other land, which are the codes CRF4A to CRF4F.
The inventory uses the point of view of the atmosphere, so a negative value is CO2 removed and a positive value is CO2 released. The accounts reverse the sign, so that a positive balance \(b\) of category \(k\) in country \(c\) is uptake. The removals \(R\) and emissions \(E\) are the two parts of that balance.
\[
R_{k,c} = \max(b_{k,c},\, 0), \qquad E_{k,c} = \max(-b_{k,c},\, 0)
\tag{1}\]
A category that is a net source in a year therefore counts fully as an emission and adds nothing to the removals of that year. Forest land can be a net source in a country. A category that a country does not report is set to zero and listed. The residual category CRF4H stays outside the account.

1.2.1 Harvested wood products
The inventory reports the change in the stock of harvested wood products as its own category, CRF4G. A deduction of that sink from the removals of forest land is one possible treatment, since the carbon in harvested wood has left the forest. The carbon chapters of Vallecillo et al. (2019) and La Notte et al. (2021) take forest uptake from the inventory as reported and make no such deduction, and the handbook of Eurostat keeps these products out of net sequestration as a separate category (Eurostat, 2026a, para. 9.56). A decision was therefore made not to deduct them. The sink stays outside the flow as a memo item.

title: Carbon sequestration
section: 1.3 The offset and the actual flow
text:
1.3 The offset and the actual flow
La Notte et al. (2021) define the service that reaches society as the balance of removals and emissions over all ecosystem types at the level of the European Union, so an ecosystem type with more emissions than removals provides no service. The EU net flow \(N\) is computed once, over all land categories and countries.
\[
N = \sum_{k,c} R_{k,c} - \sum_{k,c} E_{k,c}
\tag{2}\]
La Notte et al. (2021) then attribute this net flow to each country \(c\) in proportion to its removals of forest land \(R_{F,c}\), in their Equation 6.1. This share is the allocation key of the actual flow.
\[
F_c = N \, \frac{R_{F,c}}{\sum_{c} R_{F,c}}
\tag{3}\]
The flow without offset \(W_c\) of a country is the sum of its removals over the six land categories, and the missed flow \(M_c\) is the difference between that and the actual flow.
\[
W_c = \sum_{k} R_{k,c}, \qquad M_c = W_c - F_c
\tag{4}\]
At the level of the European Union, the missed flow equals total emissions by construction. The definition follows from the distinction that La Notte et al. (2021) draw between the role of forests, shown by removals, and the contribution to society, shown by the actual flow (see the stage accounts in the code annex).

1.3.1 Choice of the allocation key
The allocation key of Equation 3 is a choice, and a natural alternative exists. Net annual increment is the growth of living trees minus natural mortality, so it measures forest growth directly and does not depend on the sign that a category takes in the inventory. Every run compares the two keys. The compared key shares the EU net flow by the net annual increment of all forest from Eurostat (Eurostat, 2026d), with gaps filled from the nearest years of each country, and it also deducts the sink of harvested wood products from the removals of forest land. It assigns a flow to countries whose forest land is a net source and it can leave countries with a negative missed flow which has no direct reading as a service that is not delivered. The series of net annual increment also carries breaks between years, and very few countries have reported it for 2024, so most of the key of that year repeats earlier values.
A decision was made to follow Equation 6.1. Under this key no country has a negative missed flow, and a country whose forest land is a net source receives no flow, which agrees with the definition of the service. 


1.3.2 Allocation to emitting sectors
Vallecillo et al. (2019) complement the accounts with a table that attributes the actual flow of each country to the economic sectors in proportion to their share of its total CO2 emissions, which shows which sectors the service offsets. The attribution does not change the flow, and it appears in the report of each run only. We grouped the source categories of the inventory into energy supply, manufacturing and construction, transport, agriculture, forestry and fishing, households, services and other, and waste. These keep the sector names of the inventory, which differ from the industries of the national accounts, as the fuel that households burn in their cars is reported under transport.

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.4 Monetary valuation
The value of a flow is the flow in tonnes of CO2 multiplied by a price per tonne. The accounts need a price for the damage avoided by a tonne of CO2 that stays out of the atmosphere. Vallecillo et al. (2019) use the benchmark of EUR 30 per tonne of CO2 from OECD (2016), which they describe as a reference point and as a lower-end estimate. A decision was made to use a social cost of carbon instead, which is the value of the damage that one additional tonne causes, because it reflects the long-term damage of climate change and does not depend on the conditions of a carbon market in a given year.
The value draws on the meta-analysis of published estimates by Tol (2023). That work standardises every estimate to 2010 US dollars per tonne of carbon, for emissions in 2010 (Tol, 2022), and its update finds a weighted mean of 207 US$ per tonne of carbon, which rises to between 231 and 253 US$ when older studies are discounted (Tol, 2025). A decision was made to adopt 266 US$ per tonne of carbon in 2010 prices, which lies just above that range and well below the kernel mean of 509 US$ in Tol (2022), whose long right tail reflects the large uncertainty of these estimates. We moved it to 2023 prices with the consumer price index of the United States (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2023), a factor of 304.70/218.06, and to euros at the rate of 1.0813 US$ per euro in 2023 (European Central Bank, 2023). Those steps lead to about EUR 344, and the accounts use EUR 343.6 per tonne of carbon. One tonne of CO2 holds 12/44 of a tonne of carbon, so the price per tonne of CO2 is 12/44 of that value in 2023 euros (see the stage prepare in the code annex).
The social cost of carbon is a single real value, so we held it constant in 2023 euros and moved it to the prices of each year \(t\) with the harmonised index of consumer prices \(H\) of the European Union (Eurostat, 2026c). This gives the value in current prices. Constant prices of 2010 then remove general inflation, so that values of different years can be compared (see the stage accounts in the code annex).
\[
P_t = P_{2023}\, \frac{H_t}{H_{2023}}, \qquad V^{\text{current}}_{c,t} = F_{c,t}\, P_t, \qquad
V^{\text{constant}}_{c,t} = V^{\text{current}}_{c,t}\, \frac{H_{2010}}{H_t}
\tag{5}\]
 The missed flow is valued in the same way. The handbook of Eurostat does not value this service (Eurostat, 2026a).

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.5 The spatial key
The steps so far give national values. Regions and map cells receive a part of them through a spatial key, which gives each place a weight, and each place takes the national value times its share of the weight of its country.
\[
F_i = F_c\, \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j \in c} w_j}
\tag{6}\]
Because the shares of a country add up to one, regions and cells always add up to the national value, and the key decides only how that value is distributed within the country.
Vallecillo et al. (2019) map forest land only, since it is the one ecosystem type for which almost all countries report uptake, and they spread the national values with dry matter productivity over the woodland and forest of Corine Land Cover. We followed that approach, with the two more recent products that the Earth observation roadmap of the same programme names (Zurbarán Nucci et al., 2025). The weight of a place is therefore the forest on it times the productivity of its vegetation.
Forest comes from the Corine accounting layers, which the European Environment Agency prepares at 100 m for comparison between years, in version 21 for all five years (European Environment Agency, 2026). The classes are broad-leaved forest (311), coniferous forest (312), mixed forest (313) and transitional woodland and shrub (324).
Productivity is Gross Dry Matter Productivity (GDMP), the rate at which vegetation produces dry matter, estimated from satellite images by the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. The annual value is the sum of the 36 ten-day values of the year, each multiplied by its number of days. The 1 km product, version 2, covers 2000, 2006 and 2012 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-a), and it ends in 2020. The 300 m product, version 2, covers 2018 and 2024 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-b), and it starts in 2014. Since 2018 exists in both, each run compares them over the cells of 1 km that are mostly forest. A difference in level between the products changes no national total, because the key only shares a national value within a country (see the stage prepare in the code annex).
The key takes two forms, which share these ingredients and differ in resolution.

The 1 km key gives the regional tables. Its forest term \(S_i\) is the share of the 100 m cells of each 1 km cell that are forest, and its productivity \(G_i\) is the productivity on the 1 km grid, the mean of the 300 m values within each kilometre in 2018 and 2024 and the 1 km product interpolated bilinearly to the grid in the earlier years. The weight is \(w_i = S_i\, G_i\).
The 100 m key gives the maps. Its forest term is 1 for a 100 m cell of forest and 0 otherwise, and productivity is interpolated bilinearly to the 100 m grid.

Both forms place the same national totals. Within a country they agree closely, but they interpolate productivity differently, so the 100 m maps added up over a region can differ slightly from the value of that region in the tables.

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.6 Regional values
NUTS2 and NUTS3 regions receive a share of the national values (see the stage prepare in the code annex). The actual flow of a region is the national flow times the share of the region in the 1 km key of its country. The flow without offset adds up removals of six land categories, and only one of them is forest, so each category is shared in proportion to the area of that category in the region, according to the Corine accounting layer of the year. The missed flow of a region is the difference between the two. When a country has no mapped area of a category, the share of the region in the total mapped land of the country stands in.

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.7 Products
Workbook. The workbook holds one sheet for each quantity and NUTS level. The sheets of the flow without offset, the actual flow and the missed flow give thousand tonnes of CO2 and of carbon, and those of the value of the actual and the missed flow give million euro in current prices and in constant prices of 2010. The reporting years are the columns, and a first sheet explains the contents.
Maps. There are five maps for each reporting year on the 100 m grid, built with the 100 m key (see the stage maps_100m in the code annex). The first is the actual flow and the second its value at constant 2010 prices. The third is the flow without offset, for which a decision was made to map the removals of forest land, following Vallecillo et al. (2019), because other land categories switch between source and sink across years and countries and the key places forest only. This map therefore holds less than the flow without offset in the tables, which report the difference by region. The fourth and fifth are the missed flow and its value. The missed flow is a balance between removals and emissions and has no place of its own on the land, so a decision was made to allocate the national value with the key of the actual flow. These two maps show where the removals that compensate emissions are attributed, and they do not show where any loss of the service occurs.
Each cell holds a whole number in small units, kilograms of CO2 or euro cents at 2010 prices. Whole numbers take about a third of the disk of decimal numbers, and every country keeps its total to within one part in a thousand. The files are Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF without overviews, which keeps them small, and a GIS such as QGIS draws them quickly as they are.
Working layers. The run also spreads the same national values over the 1 km key. These 1 km layers are not a product of the accounts. They give the map figures of the report, drawn at 10 km, and the checks of the 1 km key against the tables (see the stage maps_1km in the code annex).

title: Carbon sequestration
text:
1.8 Checks
The run stops if any check fails. It compares the sectors with total emissions without land use, and the total of land use, CRF4, with the sum of its parts.
The 1 km layers are read back from disk and compared with the tables, and the 100 m maps are added up by country from the whole numbers as they are written and compared with the national values. The run also counts the countries that hold a flow and lack forest cells, which would lose that flow on the map.

title: Crop pollination
text: This page describes the method of the crop pollination accounts as the tool implements it. Each step points to the stage of the tool that carries it out, and the code annex at the end describes each stage with links to its code. The numbers and tables that a run produces are in the report of that run, in outputs/pollination/report/, which carries the same method text together with them.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.1 Overview
The idea behind the accounts is that wild pollinators need flowers to feed on and places to nest, and that they forage within a limited distance of both, so a crop benefits from the service only where the surrounding environment can sustain them. The accounting procedure of Vallecillo et al. (2018), which we call the method from here on, turns this idea into a chain of four components, and each one builds on the one before.
Pollination potential answers the question of how suitable a place is for wild pollinators, with a dimensionless indicator. Two groups of bees enter it, and they are known from different evidence, so the method models them separately and takes the mean. Solitary bees, which fly short distances, are described by an expert-based model that scores land cover and then corrects the score for roads, forest interiors, isolation and climate. Bumblebees are described by a species distribution model, which learns from records of where species were seenand is projected to the land cover and climate of each year. Cells with a potential of at least 0.2 form the service providing area, where pollinators are assumed to be present. Demand answers the question of where the service is needed, and it is the area of crops that benefit from insect pollination. Actual flow brings the two together, as the production attributable to pollination where demand and the service providing area overlap, and unmet demand is the same quantity where they do not. Valuation then separates the share of the value of crop production that is due to the service.
The analysis covers the European territory of the EU27, on the grid of the Corine Land Cover maps in the projection EPSG:3035, in which every cell has the same area on the ground. The inputs arrive at very different resolutions, and this shapes the processing. Land cover comes at 100 m, crops at 1 km, the bumblebee model at 10 km and climate at about 25 km. Potential is therefore modelled at 100 m, where land cover shows its detail, and combined at 1 km, the resolution of the crop data, where it can meet demand. The results are reported by region and mapped at 100 m.
Several inputs come from the public catalogue of the k.LAB project (Integrated Modelling Partnership, 2026), an open web service of harmonised layers for this same service, which a program can read directly from an address. We call it the catalogue from here on. Where a step could use more than one input, the text below says which one we chose and why. The sections follow the order of the chain.
A revision of the method was conducted in 2026 to bring two of its components up to date with newer evidence. The dependency ratios of the crops, which the method took from Klein et al. (2007), now come from the quantitative review of Siopa, Carvalheiro, Castro, Loureiro, & Castro (2024), which required a crosswalk between the crops of that review and the crop groups of the accounts. The bumblebee model, which was one layer for all years, is now projected to the land cover and climate of each reporting year from the fitted species models of 2012, which required rebuilding the layers that those models read. The sections on the bumblebee model and on the actual flow describe both changes. The accounts as they were before the revision remain available as the original method.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.2 Territory and reporting regions
The accounts are published by region, so before any modelling every kilometre of the grid has to belong to one region. We used the NUTS 2024 boundaries (Eurostat, 2024) (© EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries), the European classification of territorial units, to report by country (NUTS0), NUTS2 region and NUTS3 region. Each 1 km cell was assigned to the NUTS3 region at its centre. Coastal and border cells can have their centre outside every region while still holding crops, so they took the most common region among the cells up to 2 km away, and crop area on the coast is not lost (see the stage prepare in the code annex). All tables are built by adding up the NUTS3 regions, so the three levels match exactly. The Canary Islands, the Azores, Madeira and the overseas regions fall outside the climate data used in the model below, and they are left out.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.3 The expert-based model
The expert-based model, which Vallecillo et al. (2018) adapt from Zulian, Maes, & Paracchini (2013), scores each 100 m cell from 0 to 1 for its capacity to support wild solitary bees. It rests on what the literature and experts say about each type of land, and it uses no observations of these bees. The model starts from land cover, which indicates whether a place offers food and nesting sites. Land cover alone misses four things that also matter to a bee. A major road offers nothing, the deep interior of a forest offers less than its margin, farmland far from natural habitat receives fewer pollinators, and a cold, dull climate keeps insects in the nest. The model therefore corrects the land cover score for each of these, in the five steps below (see the stage model in the code annex).

1.3.1 Land cover
The first requirement is a land cover map that can be compared across years, because a change in the accounts should reflect a change on the ground and not a change in how the map was made. The Corine accounting layers are the versions of the Corine Land Cover maps that the European Environment Agency prepares for this kind of comparison, and they are the land cover data that the method prescribes. Two versions were within reach. The catalogue holds version 20 for the years up to 2018, whereas the Agency published version 21 for all five years in September 2026 and marked version 20 as superseded (European Environment Agency, 2026). We therefore considered two routes (see the stage fetch in the code annex).
Using the harmonised catalogue layer is the shorter route, and it also offers a ready-made map of the distance to semi-natural areas, which a later step needs. Rebuilding from primary sources means downloading version 21 and recomputing those distance maps, and it gives one consistent product across the series, including 2024. To learn whether the choice affects the results, we ran the model on both routes for 2000 and 2018 and compared them at 1 km with the same climate, road and bumblebee layers. The two agree closely on the mean and on the area served, although a few cells change substantially. Since only the rebuilt route reaches 2024, a decision was made to use it as the baseline for all years. The comparison was made once, when the route was chosen.
With the land cover map in place, the next step translates each type of land into what it offers bees. Each Corine class carries a score for floral availability \(F\) and for nesting suitability \(N\), on a scale from 0 to 1, which Zulian et al. (2013) derived from the literature and an expert workshop. A cell takes the mean of the two, as Vallecillo et al. (2018) prescribe in place of the product that Zulian et al. (2013) used. With the mean, a class that offers one resource and lacks the other keeps part of its score, whereas the product would set it to zero.
\[
S = \frac{F + N}{2}
\tag{1}\]
The scores are those of Table S1 in the supplement to Zulian et al. (2013). That article refines them with crop maps, a high resolution forest map, high nature value farmland, riparian areas and road sides, whereas the method of Vallecillo et al. (2018) works from Corine alone, so a decision was made to use the values that the supplement offers for readers who rely on Corine data only. These include an average for olive groves, which the supplement scores as 0.2 and 0.4 when intensive and 0.6 and 0.6 when extensive. We took the table from the k.LAB project (Integrated Modelling Partnership, 2026) and compared it with the supplement, and every class agrees. The scores are in the parameter file clc_pollination_scores.csv.


1.3.2 Major roads
Corine has too coarse a view to show most roads, yet major roads cannot provide food or nesting sites, so the method overlays a road network and gives cells on a major road a score of zero. It leaves local roads alone, because their margins can help pollinators or not depending on how they are managed, and that information is lacking. The network it names, TeleAtlas, is commercial and proprietary. A decision was made to use OpenStreetMap (OpenStreetMap contributors, 2026) instead, taking motorways, trunk roads and primary roads with their links, which correspond to the same categories, and marking the 100 m cells that they touch (see the stage fetch in the code annex). As in the method, the road map is a single snapshot that applies to all years.


1.3.3 Forest edges
Wild bees use forest margins more than forest interiors, but a Corine class gives one score to a whole forest patch, so the score has to be confined to the margin. Following Vallecillo et al. (2018), the outer ring of 100 m of each forest patch keeps its score and the interior scores zero. Forest means the broad-leaved, coniferous and mixed forest classes 311, 312 and 313. On a grid of 100 m the ring is one cell wide, so a forest cell belongs to the interior when all eight of its neighbours are also forest, which we tested with a moving window of three by three cells. The edge keeps the Corine score of its class from Table S1. The supplement to Zulian et al. (2013) also holds separate scores for forest edges in its Table S3, which are 0.1 higher for both floral availability and nesting suitability, and which it applies to an edge of 50 m. The method refers to the expert score of the edges without saying which table it means, and we kept Table S1.


1.3.4 Distance to semi-natural areas
A field can score well and still receive few pollinators if it lies far from the natural habitat that sustains them. Pollinator richness and visits decline exponentially with isolation from natural habitat, at a mean rate of 0.00046 per metre across 23 studies (Garibaldi et al., 2011; Ricketts et al., 2008), which halves them about every 1.5 km. The method applies this decay to the score, using the distance \(d\) in metres from each cell to the nearest semi-natural area.
\[
S_d = \exp\left(\ln(S) - 0.00046\, d\right) = S\, e^{-0.00046\, d}
\tag{2}\]
The score is zero beyond 20 km, a limit that the method sets wide on purpose so that the effect is captured over a sufficient area. Semi-natural areas are the classes 311, 312, 313, 321, 322, 323, 324, 331 and 333, which the method selects following Garibaldi et al. (2011). They change as land cover changes, so the distance is computed for each of the five land cover maps. It is the exact Euclidean distance between cell centres, searched up to 20 km around every cell, the limit beyond which the score is zero. This is the distance that the method describes (see the stage model in the code annex).


1.3.5 Activity of insects
Habitat is of no use if it is too cold for insects to leave the nest, and bees become inactive when the combination of temperature and sunshine falls below a threshold (Zulian et al., 2013). The activity index \(A\) of Corbet et al. (1993), as adapted by Zulian et al. (2013), expresses this in percent as a function of air temperature \(T\) in degrees Celsius and solar irradiance \(R\) in watts per square metre, through the temperature of a black globe that simulates the body of an insect. Its parameters were estimated for honeybees, and the method uses them as an indication for insects of similar size.
\[
A = -39.3 + 4.01\, T_b, \qquad T_b = -0.62 + 1.027\, T + 0.006\, R
\tag{3}\]
The index therefore needs monthly temperature and radiation across Europe for each period of the series. The method takes them from the Agri4Cast climate grid of about 25 km, whose radiation is a total per day, so it first has to convert that total to watts per square metre with an estimate of the hours of daylight at each latitude and date. A decision was made to use instead the ERA5 temperature (Hersbach et al., 2023) and the Copernicus radiation (Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2020) of the catalogue, on a grid of 0.25 degrees, which is of a similar size. The catalogue serves them at an open address as monthly means for the same three-year periods that the method uses, it reaches 2025, and its radiation is already expressed over day length, so no conversion is needed. A reader can also repeat this step with no account, because the tool reads the layers directly from that address.
The method is inconsistent on one point, since its text refers to minimum temperature and its table of inputs to mean temperature. The two would not give the same index, because a lower temperature lowers the result. A decision was made to use mean temperature, which is the variable in Zulian et al. (2013).
For each reporting year we took the three years centred on it, as the method does, with 2023 to 2025 for 2024, so that one unusual year does not stand for the whole period. We computed the index for each month from April to September, the months that the method chooses because they cover the sampling period of Corbet et al. (1993) and the time when pollinators visit crop flowers. The equation can return values below 0 in a cold month and above 100 in a warm one, which have no meaning as a percentage and would let one extreme month offset another, so each month was limited to the range from 0 to 100, as Zulian et al. (2013) do, before averaging the six months. The result is as coarse as the climate grid, while the model works at 100 m, so we interpolated it bilinearly to 1 km and then to 100 m (see the stage fetch in the code annex).
The four corrections come together in the expert-based model \(E\), which is the product of the decayed score and the index.
\[
E = S_d \, \frac{A}{100}
\tag{4}\]
The crop data that the model must meet exist at 1 km, so we reduced the result to that resolution, with the mean of the land cells of each kilometre, which keeps sea cells from diluting the score of a coastal kilometre. The 100 m model is kept as well, since the 100 m maps of potential use it directly. The grid holds almost two billion cells for each year, so the five steps run in tiles of 500 km, and the reduction comes out of the same pass as the 100 m model. The 100 m model of each tile is kept in the work folder for the 100 m maps stage.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.4 The bumblebee model
The second model estimates where bumblebees occur, and it works differently from the first. Where the expert-based model reasons from the scores of land cover, a species distribution model learns from observations, by relating the places where a species was recorded to the climate, land cover and terrain of those places, and then predicting where else it could live. The method fits such a model with Maxent to the records of each of 47 species on a grid of 10 km, and Polce et al. (2018) publish the result for 2012 as one layer, the mean probability of occurrence of the species present in each cell.
The published layer describes 2012, and used for every year it would leave bumblebees out of any change in the accounts. The revision of 2026 therefore projects the fitted models of the 47 species, which the Joint Research Centre keeps as Maxent files of 2012, to the land cover and climate of each reporting year. Prestele, Brown, Polce, Maes, & Whitehorn (2021) project the same models to scenarios of climate and land use in a similar way. A projection keeps each model as it was fitted and changes only the layers that it reads, so it answers the question of where the conditions that suited a species in 2012 are found in another year (see the stage sdm in the code annex).

1.4.1 Layers of each year
The models read 22 layers on the 10 km grid, and a projection needs the same layers for the year in question. The original layers are not published, so we rebuilt them from primary sources, following their description in Vallecillo et al. (2018).
Land cover. Sixteen layers give the percentage of each 10 km cell that a group of Corine classes covers, such as arable land, pastures or coniferous forest. We computed them from the Corine accounting layers of each year, the same maps that the expert-based model reads, with the groups of the method (parameter file sdm_land_classes.csv). One more layer is the mean distance to semi-natural areas within the cell, in kilometres. It is the mean of the 100 m distance of the expert-based model, limited to 20 km.
Climate. Four layers describe climate, namely temperature seasonality, the maximum temperature of the warmest month, the mean temperature of the wettest quarter and precipitation seasonality. The method derives them from the daily E-OBS grids of minimum and maximum temperature and precipitation over the 22 years from 1991 to 2012 (Cornes, Schrier, Besselaar, & Jones, 2018). We computed them in the same way for the 22 years that end in each reporting year, so 1979 to 2000 stands for 2000 and 2003 to 2024 for 2024. A window this long describes climate and not the weather of one year, and it moves slowly, since two consecutive reporting years share 16 of their 22 years. We used version 32.0e of E-OBS on its grid of 0.25 degrees, the resolution of the releases that existed when the models were fitted, and interpolated the four variables bilinearly to the 10 km grid (see the stage fetch in the code annex).
Elevation. The last layer is the most frequent elevation in each cell, which the method took from a digital elevation model of about 90 m. We computed it from the Copernicus digital elevation model of the same resolution (European Space Agency, 2024). Elevation does not change between years, so one layer serves all of them.


1.4.2 Projection
Maxent stores a fitted model as a list of features of the layers, each with a weight, and the models of the method hold hinge features only. A hinge feature is zero up to a knot and rises linearly beyond it, or the reverse. The weighted sum of the features gives the relative suitability of a cell, and the complementary log-log transformation turns it into a value between 0 and 1 that the method reads as a probability of occurrence (Phillips, Anderson, Dudík, Schapire, & Blair, 2017). We evaluated these equations directly from the model files. Every layer is first limited to the range it had when the models were fitted, the default of Maxent, so that a model is never asked about conditions it did not see. Each species has five models, from five rounds of cross-validation, and takes their mean.
The method then combines the species. A species counts as present in a cell where its probability reaches a threshold, and the value of the cell is the mean probability of the species present there. The method takes as threshold the lowest probability at any place where the species was recorded, which depends on the records and is not part of the model files. We used one threshold for all species, 0.03, the value at which the projection for 2012 comes closest to the published layer.
Open question. The thresholds of the fitted models would replace the common threshold if they become available.


1.4.3 From the projection to the layer of each year
The projection for 2012 can be compared with the published layer of 2012, which the same models gave from the original layers. The agreement confirms the reading of the models and the rebuilt layers. The difference that remains comes from what could not be reproduced exactly, namely the release of the climate grids, the elevation model and the thresholds, and it is as large as the changes of the projection between years. Replacing the published layer with the projection would therefore move the accounts of every year for reasons unrelated to bumblebees.
A decision was made to take from the projection only its change over time. The bumblebee layer \(B_y\) of year \(y\) is the published layer of 2012 plus the change of the projection \(\hat{B}\) between 2012 and that year, limited to the range from 0 to 1.
\[
B_y = B^{pub}_{2012} + \left(\hat{B}_y - \hat{B}_{2012}\right)
\tag{5}\]
Both terms of the change come from the same models and the same sources, so what the rebuilt layers miss cancels out, and 2012 keeps the published layer. The change is computed on the 10 km grid and interpolated bilinearly to 1 km, as the published layer is. A grid this coarse does not reach every stretch of coast, so land cells left without a value there took the mean of their neighbours within 10 km.

title: Crop pollination
section: 1.5 Pollination potential and the service providing area
text:
1.5 Pollination potential and the service providing area
With both groups of bees described on the same grid, the method combines them. The potential \(P\) of a 1 km cell is the mean of the expert-based model and the bumblebee model.
\[
P = \frac{E + B}{2}
\tag{6}\]
Potential is a continuous score, but the accounts need to know where the service can occur, so the method draws a line. The classes follow Vallecillo et al. (2018), namely high above 0.3, medium from 0.2 to 0.3, low from 0.1 to 0.2 and none below 0.1. Cells of medium and high potential form the service providing area, where pollinators are assumed to be present. Below that line the method assumes that they are absent, because the environment may not be enough to maintain their populations, and it presents this as a simplification for an experimental account. We added up land and agricultural land in each class by NUTS3 region (see the stage accounts in the code annex).

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.6 Demand
The other side of the account is where pollination is needed. Demand is the area of the ten crop groups in the parameter file crop_dependency.csv, which benefit from insect pollination to different degrees. This needs a map of crops, which national statistics do not provide, so the method takes the area from the CAPRI agricultural model, whose regional data are disaggregated to 1 km. The method had only two years of these data, 2004 and 2008, which do not match its years of potential. We used the later series of Koeble et al. (2024), which covers 2000 to 2018 and offers the exact reporting years. The layers were read from the catalogue, which holds the same variables for those years, and reduced to one compact stack of area and one of yield per year (see the stage fetch in the code annex). The catalogue copy was used as published, and it was not compared cell by cell with the original archives. The series ends in 2018, so the stacks of that year stand in for 2024.
Some kilometres hold more than the 100 hectares a square kilometre can contain. These values reflect multiple cropping and the way the source allocates reported land. Truncating them would understate the area, so a decision was made to keep them.

1.6.1 Countries outside the crop data
The method notes that CAPRI does not cover Croatia, Malta and Cyprus. Reading the later series gives a more nuanced picture. Croatia is absent, with a few hectares that come from cells along its border. Cyprus and Malta, by contrast, do hold crop area, and in Cyprus it is close to the national statistics. A decision was made to treat the three countries in the same way, in line with the method, so they stay out of the crop maps and take the estimate described in Section 1.7.4.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.7 Actual flow and unmet demand
Overlaying demand on the service providing area shows which crops have pollinators nearby, and the accounts then need to express this as production. Not all the production of a crop is due to insects, so the method uses a dependency ratio \(\delta_c\), the share of the production of a crop attributable to pollination. The actual flow of crop \(c\) in cell \(i\) is its production times this ratio when the cell belongs to the service providing area \(\Omega\). A cell is either inside or outside, with no gradation by level of potential. Unmet demand applies the same product to the cells outside it, so flow and unmet demand add up to all production that depends on pollination.
\[
F_{c,i} = a_{c,i}\, y_{c,i}\, k_{c}\, \delta_c \quad \text{if } i \in \Omega, \qquad
U_{c,i} = a_{c,i}\, y_{c,i}\, k_{c}\, \delta_c \quad \text{if } i \notin \Omega
\tag{7}\]
Here \(a\) is the crop area, \(y\) the yield and \(k\) a scaling factor for the crop and country, explained below. A decision was made to measure unmet demand in tonnes by analogy with the flow, because the method defines it by area only and the monetary accounts need a physical quantity. We report the area of met and unmet demand as well.

1.7.1 Dependency ratios
The method took the ratios from Klein et al. (2007), who assign each crop to a class of dependence and give the range of production loss of the class. The revision of 2026 replaced them with the values of Siopa et al. (2024), a quantitative review that derives a mean ratio for each of 141 crops from field experiments that compare flowers with and without access for pollinators. The review reports single crops, whereas the accounts work with the ten crop groups of CAPRI, so the two had to be linked with a crosswalk. A group that corresponds to one crop of the review takes its ratio, which is the case of rapeseed, soya, sunflower and tomatoes. Flax and hemp take the ratio of flax, since the review holds no value for hemp. A group of several crops takes the simple mean of the ratios of its crops that the review covers. The parameter file crop_dependency_siopa2024.csv lists the crops of each group, and crop_dependency.csv holds the resulting ratios beside those of Klein et al. (2007).
The ratios now go from 3 percent for flax and hemp to 67 percent for citrus fruits. Most groups move up, in line with the review, which finds more crops in the classes of high dependence than Klein et al. (2007) did. Citrus fruits, tomatoes, sunflower, pulses and other fruits rise the most, and apples, pears and peaches, soya, and flax and hemp fall slightly. The ratio enters the actual flow, the unmet demand and their values in direct proportion, and it leaves potential, the service providing area and the area of demand unchanged.
The mean of a group counts each of its crops once, whatever its production in the European Union.
Open question. Weighting the crops of a group by their production would lower the ratio of citrus fruits, because oranges, the main citrus crop of the European Union, have the lowest ratio of the group.


1.7.2 Scaling to national statistics
CAPRI is a model, whereas Eurostat publishes the official production of each country, and accounts are expected to agree with official figures. The method anchors its accounts in official statistics, so we compared the CAPRI production of each crop and country with the national production of Eurostat, in the three-year mean around each reporting year (Eurostat, 2026a). See the stage fetch in the code annex. The two sources can differ widely for some crops.
A decision was therefore made to keep the CAPRI pattern of each crop within a country and scale its production to the Eurostat total, with the factor \(k_c = \text{Eurostat production} / \text{CAPRI production}\). Maps and tables then agree with official totals. In 2024 the factor compares the crop pattern of 2018 with the national production around 2024, which is how national statistics reach the last year of the series. The national pollination contribution, which is the actual flow divided by total production, is unaffected by this factor, so it remains the production-weighted share that Vallecillo et al. (2018) define. Demand stays in the hectares of CAPRI, since the crop pattern on the map comes from that source. Where Eurostat has no figure for a crop and country, the CAPRI production is kept and flagged (see the stage accounts in the code annex).


1.7.3 Cases where the sources disagree on the crop
Applying the factors can expose crops and countries for which the two sources disagree on whether the crop is present at all. Scaling such cases would place unrealistic amounts in a few cells, so a decision was made to set them aside when the factor is above 10 or below 0.1. Production that Eurostat reports for these cases moves to the estimate below, and CAPRI production that Eurostat does not report is dropped.


1.7.4 Production without a place on the map
Some national production has no place on the map, either because of the countries discussed above or because of the cases just set aside. Leaving it out would make the tables fall short of the national statistics, so it needs an estimate, and with no crop map the best remaining guide is farmland. The share of the agricultural land of each region inside the service providing area stands in for the share of the crop inside it, and the agricultural land of each region shares out the national figure. Area follows the same shares, from the national area in Eurostat, and a country that reports production but no area shows flow with no hectares of demand. These values are flagged as estimates in the tables and do not enter the crop maps.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.8 Monetary valuation
Pollination contributes to a product that the national accounts already record, namely crops. The method therefore does not price the service separately. It takes the value of production in the economic accounts for agriculture and separates the part due to pollination, so no value is counted twice (Vallecillo et al., 2018). We retrieved the production value at basic price, which is what producers receive for the crop, in the prices of the previous year from Eurostat dataset aact_eaa02 (Eurostat, 2026b). The method prefers these prices to current ones so that changes reflect the biophysical side and not inflation, and it takes the mean of the three years around each reporting year to avoid odd fluctuations. Eurostat and CAPRI classify crops differently, so we linked the values to the crop groups through the correspondence in crop_dependency.csv (see the stage fetch in the code annex).
The physical accounts then say how much of each crop is due to pollination, and that share can be carried over to its value. The pollination contribution \(C\) of a crop in a country is its actual flow over its total production \(T\), and the value of the flow is the production value \(V\) times that contribution. The value of unmet demand follows in the same way.
\[
C = \frac{F}{T}, \qquad V_F = V\, C, \qquad V_U = V\, \frac{U}{T}
\tag{8}\]
Each value in the prices of the previous year has a different base year, which is a small matter between two nearby years, but these values still drift with inflation across a series of 24 years. A decision was made to express them in constant prices of 2010, since the method does not prescribe a base for a longer series, and this is the base of the carbon sequestration and wood provision accounts of the same series. We multiplied them by the deflator \(H_{2010} / \bar{H}_{y}\), where \(H\) is the harmonised index of consumer prices of the European Union (Eurostat, 2026c) and \(\bar{H}_{y}\) is its mean over the three years that the prices of each reporting year refer to. Eurostat publishes the EU27 index from 2000, and the mean of 2000 needs the two years before. Those years are estimated from the annual rates of the euro area and of the other Member States, weighted with the country weights of the first published year of the EU27 index (Eurostat, 2026c). For 2001 to 2007 the same calculation gives the published EU27 rates within 0.1 percentage points. (see the stage accounts in the code annex).
The two sources do not match perfectly. A production value in a country with no physical production has no contribution and receives no value. A country that reports production of a crop but no value for it has flow with no monetary counterpart. Regions receive the national value of each crop in proportion to their physical flow and unmet demand, through a value per tonne that is uniform within a crop and country.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.9 Maps
The tables say how much the service is worth in each region, and the maps show where it occurs. They have to tell the same story, so we built them from the same ingredients. We wrote the maps of potential, demand, actual flow, unmet demand and value at 1 km from the rasters and the factors and prices of the tables, and then read their totals back from disk to compare them with the tables (see the stage maps_1km in the code annex). These 1 km maps are working layers of the accounts and not a product in themselves. The 100 m maps are built from them.
The 100 m maps add spatial detail in two ways (see the stage maps_100m in the code annex). Potential is computed directly as the mean of the 100 m expert-based model and the bumblebee model of the same year interpolated to 100 m. The other quantities exist only at 1 km, so they are allocated within each kilometre, and each kilometre keeps its total. Demand, unmet demand and the flow and value on agroecosystems go to agricultural cells, and the flow for all ecosystem types goes to all land cells in proportion to their expert-based suitability. A kilometre with no positive weight spreads its value evenly over its land cells. The detail within each kilometre therefore comes from land cover, and crops are not observed at that scale. To make the files several times smaller, values are stored as whole numbers in small units, namely potential multiplied by 10 000, demand in square metres, flow and unmet demand in kilograms, and value in euro. They are written as Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF files without overviews, which keeps them small. A GIS such as QGIS draws them quickly as they are.
The accounts also ask which ecosystems support the service, and the flow on its own does not say, because it is measured on the crop while the pollinators depend on the land around it. To describe this, we shared the flow of each kilometre among ecosystem types in proportion to their share of its expert-based suitability, and we attributed to cropland the small amount of flow in cells with no support (see the stage maps_1km in the code annex).

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.10 Products
Workbook. The workbook holds one sheet for each group of quantities and NUTS level. The potential sheets give the hectares of land with high potential (above 0.3) and medium potential (0.2 to 0.3), on all ecosystem types and on agroecosystems. The demand sheets give the area of pollinator-dependent crops in hectares, split into met and unmet demand. The flow sheets give the actual flow and the unmet demand in tonnes, and the value sheets give both in million euro at constant prices of 2010. A last group of sheets shares the actual flow among ecosystem types, as described above. The reporting years are the columns, and each sheet states its unit and caveats in its heading.
Maps. There are eight maps for each reporting year on the 100 m grid, built as the previous section describes. They hold the potential on all ecosystem types and on agroecosystems, the demand, the actual flow on all ecosystem types and on agroecosystems, the unmet demand, and the value of the actual flow and of the unmet demand on agroecosystems. The actual flow has the same total on all ecosystem types and on agroecosystems, and the two maps place it on different cells.

title: Crop pollination
text:
1.11 Checks
A chain this long has many places where a quantity could be lost or counted twice as it passes from one step to the next, so the run tests the results as it goes and stops if any check on the tables or on the maps fails. The value of the flow in any crop and country also never exceeds the production value times the dependency ratio.
The maps agree with the tables once the estimates, which the maps leave out, are set aside. The 100 m maps as written are compared with the 1 km maps for every year (see the stage maps_100m in the code annex), and the run stops if a kilometre differs by more than the 50 units that rounding allows.
Potential can differ between the two in a kilometre, because the 100 m map interpolates the bumblebee model to 100 m rather than to 1 km. The mean of the map of potential on agricultural land is about 5 percent below that of its 1 km map because the two averages weigh cells differently. The 100 m mean counts each agricultural cell, and the 1 km mean counts each kilometre once however little agricultural land it holds.

Land cover. fetch_clc downloads the Corine accounting layers of version 21 for the five years from the record of each year in the datashare of the European Environment Agency.
Regions. fetch_gisco downloads the NUTS 2024 file at 1:1 million in EPSG:3035 from GISCO. It removes the French outermost regions (FRY) and Svalbard (NO0B2), with their parts in the regions above them, and repairs the five German regions whose boundaries cross themselves.
Roads. fetch_roads reads the motorways, trunk roads and primary roads with their links from the web feature service of the k.LAB project, page by page, and marks every 100 m cell that a road touches.
Activity index. fetch_activity reads the monthly mean temperature and radiation of each three-year window from the catalogue, computes the index of Equation 3 for each month from April to September on the climate grid, limits it to the range from 0 to 100, averages the six months and interpolates the result bilinearly to 1 km. It keeps two decimals and the land within 5 km of the EU27.
Bumblebees. fetch_sdm interpolates the published layer of 2012 bilinearly from 10 km to 1 km and fills coastal cells without a value with the mean of their neighbours in a window of 21 by 21 cells, in two passes.
Climate of the bumblebee models. fetch_eobs downloads the daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature and precipitation of E-OBS, three files of 2.1 GB together, from the server of the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute. It reduces them to monthly means and totals for each year from 1979, averages the 22 years that end in each reporting year, and computes the four bioclimatic variables with the definitions of WorldClim, where the standard deviations are those of a sample. It interpolates them bilinearly to the 10 km grid, gives cells beyond the coast of E-OBS the nearest value, writes one file of 1 MB per reporting year and removes the download.
Files inside the package. Three inputs of the bumblebee models travel with the tool and need no download. The fitted models are the 235 Maxent files of 2012, five for each of 47 species, in bumblebee_lambdas_2012.zip (0.4 MB). The mode of elevation of each 10 km cell is in elevation_mode_10km.tif (0.2 MB). It does not change between years, and building it reads about 8 GB of tiles of the Copernicus digital elevation model at 90 m (European Space Agency, 2024), so the package carries the result and elevation.py records how it was made. Each cell of the elevation model is rounded to a whole metre and counted in the 10 km cell that holds its centre, and cells of exactly 0 m, the sea of that model, are left out. The presence thresholds of the species are in bumblebee_thresholds.csv.
Crops. fetch_capri reads area and yield of the ten crop groups from the catalogue for 2000, 2006, 2012 and 2018 and writes one stack of each per year, with three decimals.
Eurostat. fetch_eurostat reads apro_cpsh1 and aact_eaa02, groups their items into the crop groups and takes the mean of the three years around each reporting year. The price index comes from prc_hicp_aind, with the years before 2000 estimated as the section on valuation explains, which also reads the country weights of prc_hicp_cow.
The fetchers write each file under a temporary name and rename it when it is complete, so an interrupted download leaves nothing half written, and esa inputs lists every input with its state. The Eurostat extracts come from the SDMX interface of Eurostat, and the fetcher records the date of retrieval of each one in extracts.json beside it, since a new release can revise past values. The report of each run lists the inputs with those dates.

prepare
inputs.py, nuts.py · esa run pollination -s prepare
Reads the NUTS 2024 regions of the EU27, numbers the NUTS3 regions in order of their code and rasterises them on the 1 km grid, where each cell takes the region at its centre. Cells on the coast whose centre falls outside every region take the most common region within 2 km, with ties going to the smallest number.

title: Crop pollination
text:
model
inputs.py, model.py · esa run pollination -s model
Runs the expert-based model at 100 m in tiles of 500 km, in parallel. Each tile reads Corine, the major roads and the activity index, computes the exact distance to semi-natural areas with a margin of 20 km, applies the five steps of the model and masks the result to the EU27. The same pass reduces the model to 1 km, with the mean over land and over farmland, the number of land and farmland cells and the sum on each ecosystem type, which the later stages read. It also keeps the 100 m model of each tile in work/pollination/prep/ebm_100m/, about 1 GB a year, for the 100 m maps.

title: Crop pollination
text:
sdm
sdm.py, maxent.py · esa run pollination -s sdm
Builds the bumblebee layer of each reporting year. For each year it computes the land cover layers of the species models on the 10 km grid, in tiles of 500 km and in parallel, namely the percentage of each cell in sixteen groups of Corine classes and the mean distance to semi-natural areas, and keeps them in work/pollination/prep/. It reads the climate layers of the year from the store and the elevation layer from the package, and rounds land cover, climate and elevation to whole numbers, as the layers of the fitted models were. maxent.py reads the model files and evaluates them with NumPy, with no Java. It accepts linear and hinge features, limits each layer to the range of the fitted model, and returns the complementary log-log output. The stage takes the mean of the five models of each species, counts a species as present at or above its threshold, and takes the mean probability of the species present.
The layer of a year is the published layer of 2012 plus the change of this projection since 2012 (Equation 5), interpolated bilinearly from 10 km to 1 km and limited to the range from 0 to 1. The stage also projects the land cover of each year with the climate of 2012, and the reverse, for the table that separates the two drivers, and it compares the projection for 2012 with the published layer. Each projection is redone only when its code, its parameters or its input files change.

accounts
tables.py, model.py · esa run pollination -s accounts
Adds the 1 km layers up by NUTS3 region, scales the CAPRI crops to Eurostat production, estimates the production without a place on the map, builds the physical accounts, values them with the economic accounts for agriculture and deflates them to 2010 prices. It writes the small tables of the report and stops if a check fails.

title: Crop pollination
text:
maps_100m
maps.py · esa run pollination -s maps_100m
Reads the 100 m model that the model stage kept for each tile and the bumblebee layer of the year, and writes eight maps per year as whole numbers, which allocate the 1 km values within each kilometre. Each tile compares its maps with the 1 km maps, and the tiles are joined into Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF files without overviews. Each tile goes through in strips of 20 km, which keeps the arrays small enough for the processor cache.
